description: We are a team of aspiring innovators and engineering students from Kerala, India, interested in space exploration, technology, software development, and scientific storytelling. Our goal is to transform NASA's space mission data into an engaging and educational digital experience that helps people understand the history and scientific importance of equipment left on the Moon and Mars.
summary:
After the Landing is a website that explores the objects and equipment humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars during space missions. We usually focus on the discoveries made by astronauts, landers and rovers, but we rarely think about what happens to the equipment after a mission ends.

Through this project, we bring together information about these objects from different NASA missions, including Apollo, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Perseverance and InSight. The website allows visitors to explore these missions, learn about the objects left behind and understand their history through images and information.

Our aim is to make space exploration more interesting and help people discover a side of space missions that is often overlooked. These objects may no longer be active, but they still represent important achievements in human exploration and scientific history.
details:
AFTER THE LANDING — Space Heritage Explorer

After the Landing, created by ANKH, is an interactive, cinematic educational archive that explores the human-made objects, scientific instruments and historical traces left behind on the Moon and Mars by space exploration missions.

While space missions are often remembered for their launches, landings and discoveries, the hardware and equipment left behind tell another important story. Our project brings this overlooked aspect of space exploration to life through an immersive digital experience.

What does the project do and how does it work?

The platform provides an interactive archive of 18 mission-related objects from lunar and Martian exploration. Users can explore dedicated Moon and Mars sections, discover individual mission objects, learn about their original purposes, understand their scientific contributions and examine their historical significance.

Each object has a dedicated information page containing its mission context, purpose, status, facts and legacy. The platform also features an interactive mission timeline, archive filters, educational content and animated planetary environments.

It distinguishes between deliberately impacted spacecraft, discarded landing hardware, scientific equipment and still-operational rovers, helping users understand the different categories of human-made objects on other worlds.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging.
  • Educates users about the scientific instruments and technologies used in lunar and Martian missions.
  • Preserves awareness of historical human activity beyond Earth.
  • Helps students and space enthusiasts understand the long-term legacy of space exploration.
  • Presents scientific and historical information through an easy-to-navigate visual archive.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to create awareness of humanity’s growing footprint beyond Earth and encourage people to look beyond the achievements of landing on another world.

Every object left behind represents engineering, scientific discovery and a moment in human exploration. By documenting these objects, we hope to encourage curiosity about planetary exploration, space heritage and the importance of preserving the history of our activities on other celestial bodies.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a lightweight, responsive web application using:

  • HTML5 – Structure and content.
  • CSS3 – Responsive layouts, visual design, animations and transitions.
  • JavaScript – Interactive features, navigation, archive filtering and dynamic content.
  • NASA Images API – Research and retrieval of representative space mission imagery.
  • Solar System Scope textures – Planetary surface textures for immersive visual environments.
  • GitHub Pages – Public hosting and deployment.

All 18 project photographs are stored locally within the project. The website does not require a backend, database, npm installation or external JavaScript libraries.

How is the project creative and innovative?

Instead of presenting space mission information as a conventional list of facts, After the Landing transforms it into a cinematic digital heritage experience.

The platform combines animated planetary environments, editorial storytelling, interactive mission-object dossiers, a colour-coded timeline and a searchable archive. Its Moon and Mars sections have distinct visual identities and educational content.

A key feature is its classification of deployed scientific equipment, discarded landing components, deliberately impacted hardware and active mission vehicles. This provides a clearer and more scientifically responsible understanding of what remains on these worlds.

What factors did we consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, historical context, accessibility, responsive design, performance and educational value throughout development.

Particular attention was given to distinguishing active mission hardware from abandoned or discarded objects, correctly representing mission events and providing appropriate image-source credits.

The website supports desktop and mobile devices, keyboard navigation and reduced-motion preferences. Local image storage also helps maintain availability without relying on external image servers.

After the Landing is more than an archive of objects. It is a digital record of humanity’s journey beyond Earth and the stories we leave behind.
